title: When to use LinkedList over ArrayList: decision guide
shortTitle: When should you use LinkedList over ArrayList?
keyPoints: ArrayList is the default choice for 95% of use cases because of CPU cache locality and lower memory overhead
LinkedList is better only when you insert/remove at the current ListIterator position during traversal
For queue (FIFO) and stack (LIFO) behavior, ArrayDeque outperforms LinkedList in both speed and memory
Never use LinkedList when you need random access by index; get(i) is O(n) versus O(1) for ArrayList
LinkedList uses 8-10x more memory per element than ArrayList due to Node object overhead
Even add(0, elem) on ArrayList can be faster than LinkedList in practice because System.arraycopy is CPU-optimized

s1_definition.oneliner: Use ArrayList as the default; use LinkedList only when you need O(1) insert/remove at the current ListIterator position during traversal, and never for random access or queue/stack operations.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **ArrayList (default choice)**: fast random access O(1), excellent cache locality, compact memory (~4 bytes/element), amortized O(1) add at end
- **LinkedList (niche choice)**: O(1) insert/remove during ListIterator traversal, O(1) operations at both ends, implements both List and Deque
- **ArrayDeque (for queue/stack)**: faster than LinkedList for Deque operations, contiguous memory, no node object overhead
- The decision flow: need random access? ArrayList. Need queue/stack? ArrayDeque. Need ListIterator modification? LinkedList.
s1_definition.analogy: In a bank branch, ArrayList is the digital screen showing customer numbers in order – instant lookup by position, and adding a new number at the end takes a moment. LinkedList is a paper chain where each slip points to the next – easy to insert a slip anywhere in the chain during a walk-through, but finding slip number 500 means counting from the start. ArrayDeque is the modern electronic queue system – fast for calling the next customer and efficient with resources.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Decision flowchart: which List implementation?

  Need get/set by index?
  ├── YES → ArrayList
  └── NO
        Need queue/stack (FIFO/LIFO)?
        ├── YES → ArrayDeque
        └── NO
              Insert/remove during iteration?
              ├── YES → LinkedList
              └── NO
                    Need List + Deque interfaces?
                    ├── YES → LinkedList
                    └── NO  → ArrayList (safe default)

  Performance reality check:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ArrayList wins for:                         │
  │  - Random access (O(1) vs O(n))            │
  │  - Iteration (cache locality)              │
  │  - Memory (4 bytes vs 40 bytes/element)    │
  │  - Small-medium lists (< 100K elements)    │
  │                                             │
  │ LinkedList wins for:                        │
  │  - ListIterator insert/remove (O(1))       │
  │  - Very large lists with frequent head ops │
  │                                             │
  │ ArrayDeque wins for:                        │
  │  - Queue operations (faster + less memory) │
  │  - Stack operations (faster than Stack)    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The ArrayList vs LinkedList decision is simpler than most developers think. ArrayList is the right choice for 95% of use cases. Its contiguous memory layout gives it a massive CPU cache advantage that makes it faster even for operations where LinkedList has better theoretical complexity.

LinkedList has exactly one genuine advantage: O(1) insert and remove at the current ListIterator position during traversal. If you are walking through a list and need to add audit entries or remove flagged items inline, LinkedList does this without shifting elements. Every other scenario – random access, iteration, queue behavior, stack behavior – has a better alternative.

For queue and stack operations, use ArrayDeque. It is faster than LinkedList because its circular array is cache-friendly, and it uses 10x less memory because it does not create a Node object for each element.

In the National Bank of India system, Rajesh uses ArrayList for transaction histories because he needs paginated access. He uses ArrayDeque for the transaction processing queue because it handles FIFO efficiently. He uses LinkedList only in the compliance scanning module where the auditor walks through transactions with a ListIterator and inserts hold notes after suspicious entries.

Remember one sentence: ArrayList is the default, ArrayDeque is for queues and stacks, and LinkedList is only for ListIterator-based modification during traversal.
